findings.title: Web actuator endpoints ship with show-values: always, letting any authenticated ROLE_USER read the JWT signing secret and admin password; the stolen HMAC secret allows offline pinpointJwt forgery and ROLE_ADMIN escalation on /api/admin/**
findings.preconditions: Stock deployment with the documented basic-login mode enabled (pinpoint.modules.web.login=basicLogin, the vendor-recommended authentication mode). Attacker holds any valid low-privilege ROLE_USER account. The actuator management server is reachable to the attacker (management.server.port=8443, bound by default in the shipped web-starter configuration; no role rule restricts /monitor). No administrator misconfiguration is required: management.endpoint.env/configprops show-values: always and the missing /monitor-specific authorization rule are shipped defaults in web-starter/src/main/resources/application.yml.
findings.positiveControl: Authenticated ROLE_USER GET http://<web>:8443/monitor/env returned HTTP 200 with 34,728 bytes of Spring Environment properties including the configured values web.security.auth.jwt.secretkey, web.security.auth.user, web.security.auth.admin and admin.password verbatim (dummy values planted for the test were all found byte-for-byte). Using the read secret, an HS256 pinpointJwt with userId=<admin-username> and userRole=[ROLE_ADMIN] was forged offline; with that cookie GET /api/admin/agentIdMap returned HTTP 200 whereas the same request with a real ROLE_USER cookie returned HTTP 403 and with no cookie returned HTTP 302.
findings.negativeControl: Anonymous GET /monitor/env on 8443 returned HTTP 302 redirect to /login (the basic-login filter chain covers the management server). A request carrying a garbage pinpointJwt cookie to the same URL also returned 302. The privilege-escalation step was differential: forged-admin cookie 200 vs real-ROLE_USER-cookie 403 vs no-cookie 302 on the identical /api/admin request.
findings.observedImpact: Full privilege escalation from ROLE_USER to ROLE_ADMIN on the web application: the forged token grants /api/admin/** (destructive admin operations such as application/agent data deletion), and the same env output discloses admin.password used by the second admin gate. The JWT secret also allows minting tokens for any username for the 12-hour token lifetime (logout only deletes the cookie; there is no server-side revocation).
findings.notDemonstrated: Not demonstrated: destructive /api/admin write operations were not executed (the escalation proof uses one read-only authenticated route whose authorization outcome differs by cookie state: 302/403/500); impact on deployments where basic login is disabled (app is then anonymous by a separate documented design) was not tested; exploitation was performed only against the local Docker lab; no released-version sweep. A transient 302-flap of the lab under sibling-container load is documented in evidence/f1-flap-note.txt.

findings.title: Shipped server.error configuration (include-exception/message/binding-errors/stacktrace: always) plus an in-repo @ControllerAdvice disclose full internal stack traces and request parameters to unauthenticated callers via the permitAll /api-public/error path
findings.preconditions: Stock deployment; the error-disclosure settings and the /api-public permitAll error path are shipped defaults in web-starter/src/main/resources/application.yml and web/src/main/resources/problem/. Attacker needs only network reachability to the web port; no account is required.
findings.positiveControl: Anonymous GET /api-public/error on the stock web container returned HTTP 200 with an RFC 7807 body whose trace property contained a full ~60-frame Java stack trace (internal package names, Spring Security filter chain classes, Tomcat internals), and whose properties echoed the request method, parameters and the container hostname.
findings.negativeControl: The same request was confirmed to hit the public path without authentication by design (permitAll rule for /api-public/** in basic-login/src/main/java/.../PinpointBasicLoginConfig.java). Negative control for the disclosure knob itself is source-level: setting include-stacktrace to never removes the trace property (Spring Boot ErrorAttributes behavior); this knob-off state was not separately run in the lab and is recorded under Not demonstrated.
findings.observedImpact: Unauthenticated disclosure of internal class names, library versions, filter-chain structure, absolute framework internals and request-echoed parameters. Useful for reconnaissance in chained attacks; no direct confidentiality breach of business data was observed.
findings.notDemonstrated: Not demonstrated: the knob-off negative control was not executed in the lab; no business-data leakage via this path was shown; stack traces from exception-carrying endpoints (e.g. storage failures) were not triggered because HBase was unavailable in the lab, so only the framework-level 404 handler output was captured.

findings.title: Collector serves Spring Boot actuator endpoints (env/configprops with show-values: always, writable loggers) under /monitor on its main HTTP port 8081 with no authentication, while the same application password-gates /admin/** on the same port
findings.preconditions: Stock deployment of the collector (exposure list, show-values: always and loggers access: unrestricted are shipped defaults in collector/src/main/resources/application.yml and collector-starter/src/main/resources/application.yml). Attacker needs only network reachability to collector HTTP port 8081; no account, no operator misconfiguration. The vendor's own quickstart maps 8081 and configures path-mapping.health=l7check, indicating the port is meant to be reachable by infrastructure.
findings.positiveControl: Anonymous GET /monitor/env returned HTTP 200, 40,145 bytes, with the researcher-planted collector.admin.password, JDBC password and Redis password appearing verbatim (verify-admin-pw / verify-dummy-pw / verify-redis-pw), across all property sources including command-line -D values. Anonymous GET /monitor/loggers/<name> returned 200; anonymous POST {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"} returned 204 and the change was confirmed by a second anonymous read (configuredLevel DEBUG), then reverted to INFO. All credentials in evidence are planted dummies.
findings.negativeControl: The same anonymous client, same port, requested /admin/enableAccess and was refused (401/403 by AuthInterceptor) — the gate exists, only for the other surface. pause is listed in exposure.include but does not resolve on the shipped collector (POST /monitor/pause 404, absent from the /monitor link list).
findings.observedImpact: Unauthenticated disclosure of every secret held in the collector process environment — including the admin password that unlocks the gated /admin/** surface on the same port, and the database/cache credentials the collector uses — plus an unauthenticated runtime log-level write.
findings.notDemonstrated: Not demonstrated: external routability of port 8081 is operator- and network-dependent; no destructive /admin operation was attempted with the read password; no released-version sweep beyond the 4.0.0 image (the exposure block entered with commit 8264ec0659, first released in v3.1.0, per the full-history trace in the audit notes).

findings.title: OTLP metric ingestion POST /opentelemetry buffers and parses unauthenticated request bodies with no size, in-flight or concurrency bound, while the sibling OTLP/HTTP endpoints /v1/traces and /v1/logs in the same release enforce a 4 MiB per-request cap, a 256 MiB in-flight budget and a 64-request gate
findings.preconditions: Stock deployment: the module is enabled by shipped default in collector-starter/src/main/resources/application.yml (pinpoint.modules.collector.otlpmetric.enabled: true). Attacker needs only network reachability to the collector HTTP port; no account. Verification method (stated honestly): a fixture process assembled from the RELEASED 4.0.0-metric artifacts (real OpenTelemetryMetricController, real ProtobufHttpMessageConverter, real OtlpTraceHttpAdmissionFilter as the sibling control, embedded Tomcat, -Xmx128m, bound to 127.0.0.1 only) with only the storage service stubbed — the claim lives between the socket and the parsed message, which is unstubbed. Recipe: env/fixture-c8/README.md.
findings.positiveControl: Valid ExportMetricsServiceRequest bodies (pure-stdlib encoder, wire-checked) of 1/8/32/64 MiB were each accepted with HTTP 200 — no 413, no 503, no Retry-After at any size; a single 64 MiB request drove live heap from ~46 MiB to ~113 MiB of the 128 MiB ceiling. Three concurrent 32 MiB requests produced two HTTP 500s with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space logged with the stack inside ExportMetricsServiceRequest$Builder.mergeFrom -> Arrays.copyOfRange — the OOM occurs in the parse itself, upstream of any storage step.
findings.negativeControl: The identical 8 MiB body sent to /v1/traces in the same fixture process is answered HTTP 413 by the shipped OtlpTraceHttpAdmissionFilter (4 MiB cap) — same server, same port, same bytes: one path refuses, the other buffers fully. 1 MiB to /v1/traces returns 200 (admitted), confirming the control path is live rather than 404.
findings.observedImpact: An unauthenticated client chooses how much collector heap a request consumes; concurrent oversized bodies exhaust the JVM heap and stop the collector's ingestion and admin work for every other client.
findings.notDemonstrated: Not demonstrated: the production -Xmx threshold at which real deployments OOM (the fixture deliberately used a small ceiling); the full collector stack with real Pinot/Kafka could not be started in the lab (pinpoint-hbase:4.0.0 HMaster deadlocks on arm64 — see Limitations); the synthetic payloads omit the pinpoint.agentId resource attribute, so the mapper skips the datapoints (savedDatapoints=0) — irrelevant to the observation, which is in the parse layer; no released-version sweep beyond the 4.0.0-metric artifacts (module introduced by commit 7f5df185c9, first released in v3.0.1).
